P000.why: Balancing figures on a lever (centres of gravity) is used to discover area and volume results later proved by exhaustion.

ms.l: Democritus asserts the cone and pyramid volumes
ms.d: Democritus first stated that cone and pyramid are one third of cylinder and prism, a result Archimedes says he discovered by his method.

ev.c: Democritus was first to assert these volumes; Eudoxus first proved them.
ev.s: Heath, The Method of Archimedes (1912), introduction

ms.l: Quadrature of the Parabola outlines the mechanical method
ms.w: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola (letter to Dositheus)
ms.d: Archimedes gives the area of a parabolic segment first by a lever argument and then by exhaustion.

ev.c: He first outlines the mechanical proof in Quadrature of the Parabola next to the geometric one, and gives a fuller account in The Method.
Heath's order places the Parabola before the Method.

ms.l: Mechanical discovery of the parabola's area
ms.w: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola
ms.d: The lever argument is used to find the area of a parabolic segment, later confirmed by exhaustion.

ev.c: Same source as above: the mechanical argument appears alongside the geometric proof.

ms.w: Archimedes, Method concerning mechanical theorems, letter to Eratosthenes
ms.d: Archimedes explains in a letter how balancing slices of figures led him to results such as sphere and cylinder volumes, which he then proved by exhaustion.

ev.c: It is a letter to Eratosthenes and holds the first attested explicit use of indivisibles.
ev.s: Wikipedia, The Method of Mechanical Theorems

ev.c: Archimedes states that some results became clear by a mechanical method before geometric proof.
Heath's 1912 English edition (scanned).

ms.l: Heiberg finds the Method in a palimpsest
ms.w: J. L. Heiberg, discovery of the Archimedes Palimpsest, summer 1906
ms.d: Heiberg recognised a tenth-century prayer book as carrying Archimedes' lost Method, so the text reached modern readers.

ev.c: In the summer of 1906 Heiberg discovered the manuscript that includes The Method.
The work was thought lost until its rediscovery in the palimpsest in 1906.
ev.s: Wikipedia, The Method of Mechanical Theorems

ms.w: T. L. Heath, The Method of Archimedes (Cambridge, 1912)

ev.c: Internet Archive record of the 1912 edition.

ms.l: Law of the lever and centres of gravity

ms.d: The mechanical method rests on the lever law and centres of gravity proved in this earlier treatise.

ev.c: The mechanical method relies on the centroid and lever law demonstrated in On the Equilibrium of Planes.

works.c: Netz, The Archimedes Codex (2007)

P003.why: The problem of points and dice questions are solved by counting equally likely cases, then generalised into a calculus of chance and, with Laplace, an analytic one.

ms.w: Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica, geometrica, proportioni et proportionalita, 1494
ms.d: Early printed treatment of the interrupted game that divided the stake by rounds already won, a rule Tartaglia later criticised; neither used counting of future outcomes.
ms.ph: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)

ev.c: Pacioli treated the interrupted game in 1494 by proportion to rounds won; Tartaglia found the rule defective.

ms.w: Girolamo Cardano, Liber de ludo aleae, written 1560s, printed 1663
ms.d: Cardano counted outcomes of dice throws in the 1560s, but the text circulated only in print about a century later.

ev.c: Cardano's dice work dates from the 1560s and was not published until around 100 years later.

ms.l: Pascal-Fermat correspondence solves the problem of points by counting equally likely futures
ms.w: Pascal-Fermat letters, summer 1654
ms.d: In five letters the two settled the division of stakes by counting the equally likely ways the game could have continued, introducing what is effectively expectation.
ms.ph: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)

ev.c: Their correspondence of summer 1654 treated the dice problem and the problem of points.
Fermat's method counted the equally likely continuations; Pascal gave a step-by-step recursion and a binomial formula.

ms.l: Huygens' printed treatise on reasoning in games of chance
ms.w: Christiaan Huygens, De ratiociniis in ludo aleae, in F. van Schooten, Exercitationum mathematicarum, 1657
ms.d: The first published treatise devoted to probability, solving gambling problems by an expectation principle.

ev.c: Archive.org record dates De ratiociniis in ludo aleae to 1657.
Huygens' 1657 text is described as the first published book wholly on probability.
MacTutor reproduces the first page of De ratiociniis in ludo aleae (1657).

ms.l: Ars conjectandi and the law of large numbers

ev.c: Archive.org records list the 1713 Basel edition.
Ars Conjectandi (1713) introduced the law of large numbers.

P004.why: A puzzle about walks across bridges is stripped to vertices and edges, and a parity condition settles it, an early instance of 'geometry of position'.

ms.l: Euler presents the solution to the St Petersburg Academy
ms.w: Euler, talk of 26 August 1735
ms.d: The solution was presented to the Academy six years before it was printed.

ev.c: Euler's work was presented to the St Petersburg Academy on 26 August 1735

ms.w: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis, Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 8 (1736), printed 1741
ms.d: Euler recasts the bridge puzzle as land masses and links, shows the walk is impossible and states the parity rule for general networks; history pages regard it as the first paper in graph theory.
ms.ph: Euler and the geometry of position

ev.c: Published in the St Petersburg Commentarii in 1741; mathematical formalisation and proof of impossibility laid the foundations of graph theory

ms.n: Use of graph structure for a target problem outside pure combinatorics; the paper content itself was not read. Treated as the earliest application of the graph viewpoint, not as the start of the subject.

P428.why: Hamilton's decade-long search for a multiplication on three-dimensional space ended in the four-dimensional non-commutative quaternions, the first prominent non-commutative number system, taken up in physics by Tait.

ms.l: Hamilton treats complex numbers as ordered pairs
ms.w: W. R. Hamilton, algebraic couples, read to the Royal Irish Academy 1833
ms.d: Hamilton presents complex numbers as a two-dimensional system over the reals, then spends about ten years seeking a three-dimensional analogue.

ev.c: Topic page says he presented this to the Irish Academy in 1833 and then tried to define a product on 3-space.

ms.l: Discovery of the quaternion rules, 16 October 1843

ms.d: Hamilton realises that the product on triples fails but a four-dimensional non-commutative system works, and records i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1.

ev.c: Biography dates the discovery to 16 October 1843 and calls quaternions the first non-commutative algebra studied.

ms.n: Hamilton also communicated the discovery to the Royal Irish Academy in November 1843 (printed in its Proceedings); that earlier record was not checked, so 1844 is the earliest verified print.

ev.c: Crossref gives vol. 25, pp. 10-13, dated July 1844, for the first part; later parts have DOIs 10.1080/14786444408644984 and 10.1080/14786444408645047.
Article says quaternions were introduced by Hamilton in 1843 (announcement) with the series following.
